page.title: OpenGEO Findings
page.description: What gets a page cited by AI answer engines, by how much, and how sure we are — from an open, reproducible benchmark.
eyebrow: open benchmark for AI answer engines
page.headline: Specific facts are what get a page cited by AI answer engines.
page.standfirst: OpenGEO changes one thing about a document and measures whether the models behind {engine_names} cite it more. Adding specific figures took a page from being cited {facts_pooled_control_pct0} of the time to {facts_pooled_treatment_pct1}, on every model tested. Repeating keywords moved it by {stuffing_pooled_delta_abs} points. Every number carries its interval, and the tests that found nothing are reported alongside the ones that did.
page.hero_caption: What changing a page did to its citation rate
page.hero_note: Both changes were measured against the same kind of starting page — one that doesn't answer the question, cited {baseline_range} of the time. Pages with facts were cited {facts_pooled_treatment_pct1} of the time, so the specific-facts effect ran into the ceiling: its direction is clear, but its size reflects where the vague page started and is not identified.
page.limits_heading: What this can't tell you yet
limits: Whether your page gets found in the first place. We hand each engine six documents and measure what it does with them. Search ranking and retrieval are held constant on purpose, and are a separate experiment.

Which presentation tactic is best. At the stage measured here, answer-first order, FAQ headings, attribution and source citations did not move citation, and ranking them would need documents cut in a way that turned out to be an artefact. If they help, they help a page get found, which is a different experiment.
How real, published pages behave. Test documents are written for the benchmark so that exactly one thing changes between versions.
How the engines' own websites behave, beyond the single early check above.

method.text: Six candidate sources per question. Only the page under test differs between versions; the other five are byte-identical.
{runs_per_cell} runs per question per engine, at default randomness, with source order shuffled every run.
Rounds marked pre-registered published their hypothesis and analysis plan before a single call was made.
Split-half reliability {reliability_low}–{reliability_high} per engine. Documents, code and every raw response are public.

page.footer: Every figure on this page is read from results/findings.json, which cites the committed report each one comes from, and the page is regenerated when a round closes. Code MIT, data and results CC-BY 4.0. Engines are tested through the API models named on each chart.

findings.title: Put the specific answer on the page
findings.lever: Replace vague claims with specific figures

chart.aria: Citation rate per engine for the vague and the specific version of each page

body: We took pages that talk around a question and replaced their generic phrasing with the specific figure the question asks for — a price, an interval, a dose — keeping the length within three words. Citation rose on every model we tested, by {delta_min_abs} to {delta_max_abs} points. The same result appeared at {replication_prompts} questions and again at {prompts}.
text.caption: Share of runs in which each engine cited the page. Engines ordered by share of AI-assistant web traffic ({share_source}). {others_effect_sentence}; the pooled {pooled_delta_pts} points {pooled_ci_pts} covers all {n_models} models.
text.for_you: Where a page says “fast,” “affordable” or “most teams,” say how fast, how much, and how many.

findings.title: Repeating your keyword helps a little, and doesn't get you misquoted

moonshotai/kimi-k2.excluded: failing to cite sources reliably (no-cite rate 12.1%)

fidelity.metric: share of cited sentences the page does not support (stuffed − orthogonal, per-prompt paired)

chart.aria: Change in citation rate from keyword repetition per engine, with 95% intervals

body: We expected keyword stuffing to do nothing, or to hurt. It helped: repeating a page's topic phrase four to eight times, with no new facts and no extra length, raised citation by {pooled_delta_pts} points {pooled_ci_pts} — roughly {ratio_vs_compare}× smaller than the effect of adding specific figures. No engine went significantly the other way{panel_spans_zero_clause}.
text.caption: Change in citation rate from repetition, with 95% intervals. Dots in green have intervals clear of zero. The pooled figure covers {n_models} models, as the pre-registration specified — {others_pool_sentence}. {excluded_sentence}
after: We also checked whether stuffed pages get misrepresented more once cited. They don't: the share of attributed claims the page didn't support moved by {fidelity_delta_pts} points {fidelity_ci_pts}, and a second, independent judge model agreed.
text.for_you: Naming your topic plainly helps a little. It is the weaker lever by an order of magnitude — facts first.

findings.title: Padding a page with filler does not win it citations
findings.lever: Double the word count, add no facts

chart.aria: Change in citation rate from doubling a page's length with filler, per engine, with 95% intervals

body: Doubling a page's length with filler that states no fact, names no entity and repeats none of the question's words moved its citation rate by {pooled_delta_pts} points {pooled_ci_pts} — an interval comfortably around zero. Length is invisible in this round's variance decomposition too, behind which question was asked, which domain it came from, and the page's format.

But the engines disagree about the sign. On {n_negative} of the five a padded page is cited less often, each with an interval clear of zero, and two of those hold up after correcting across the panel. The engines that shrug padding off are the two carrying most of the traffic, which is why the pooled figure lands flat. Nothing here rewards padding on any engine; on some it costs you.
text.caption: Change in citation rate from doubling length with filler, with 95% intervals. Dots in red have intervals entirely below zero. Pooled across {n_models} engines, weighted by market share. {excluded_sentence}
after: A page's share of the answer's sentences — a fairer test of the word-count metrics used elsewhere in this field — did not move either, on any dose.
text.for_you: Words are not the lever. Adding length without adding facts is at best neutral, and on several engines it actively costs you citations.

findings.title: How the answer is presented does not change whether it is cited
findings.lever: Answer-first order, FAQ headings, attribution, source citations

chart.aria: Change in citation rate from four presentation tactics, per engine, with 95% intervals

body: These are the things the optimisation advice actually sells: put the answer first, format it as an FAQ, attribute it to its source, cite where it came from. We applied all four to documents already competing against real alternatives, holding the facts identical — no tactic was allowed to add a figure the original did not have, because a page that says more is already known to win. Pooled across the panel they moved citation by {pooled_delta_pts} points {pooled_ci_pts}.

The engines are not unanimous, and the disagreement is worth more than the pooled figure. On one engine these tactics cost a page citations and on another they earn a few, each with an interval clear of zero — but neither survives correction across the panel, and they point opposite ways. Per-cell movement sat at the level you get from running the same unchanged document twice.
text.caption: Change in citation rate from four fact-preserving presentation tactics, with 95% intervals. Pooled across {n_models} engines, weighted by market share. {prompts} questions — an estimate with an interval, not a published effect size.
after: Two further probes asked whether the documents were simply too short for order to matter. Lengthening them did not rescue the effect. Rebuilding every document as a full page section did something more awkward: the citation rates split to the extremes, most documents either always cited or never, and the gradeable middle this measurement depends on disappeared.

That middle turns out to be an artefact of cutting the documents short. A short excerpt is a partial answer and earns a partial rate; a full page either contains the answer or it does not. So this null cannot be fixed by running a bigger version of it — the regime it needs is a property of the truncation, not of the content.
text.for_you: Presentation is not the lever at this stage. What the engine does with a page it already has depends on whether the page answers the question, not on where the answer sits or how it is framed. If these tactics help, they help earlier — by getting the page retrieved at all — and that is not what this measures.
prov: design and reading committed before collection
fact-preserving by construction: no tactic adds a figure

provenance.round: tactic pilot, length ladder, page-length screen

findings.title: Engines largely agree on what deserves a citation

data.metric: Kendall's W on per-document citation rates, against a within-model split-half floor

labels: Different engines, compared with each other
One engine, compared with its own re-run
chart.aria: Kendall's W between engines, and within one engine against its own re-run

body: GEO tools are often sold on the idea that every engine is its own optimisation problem. We measured how closely engines agree on which documents they cite, and compared it with how closely one engine agrees with itself when asked the same thing again. Engines agree with each other about as closely as one engine agrees with its own re-run — the disagreement between them is no bigger than ordinary run-to-run noise.
text.caption: Kendall's W: the higher it is, the more alike two rankings of which documents get cited. The within-engine figure is the noise floor any real disagreement would have to clear. {latest_label} shown; the {earlier_label} gave {earlier_cross} against {earlier_within}.
text.for_you: A page that earns citations from one engine tends to earn them from the others. The data doesn't support a separate strategy per engine.
prov: measured on two independent document sets

findings.title: Engines sometimes credit your page with things it doesn't say

data.metric: share of cited sentences a judge finds the page does not support (NOT_SUPPORTED)
data.method: fidelity_baseline.py — clean judgments only, last row per item, bootstrap over prompts, 10,000 resamples, seed 20260830

chart.aria: {low_n} per 100 cited sentences unsupported by the more lenient judge's count, {high_n} per 100 by the stricter judge's
chart.legend_low: {low_n}  per 100 by the more lenient judge's count ({low_judge}, 95% CI {low_ci})
chart.legend_high: {high_n}  per 100 by the stricter judge's count ({high_judge}, 95% CI {high_ci})
chart.legend_rest: supported, or partly supported, by the page

body: Being cited isn't the same as being represented accurately. For every sentence that cited a page, we asked a separate model whether the page actually supports it. Between {low_pct} and {high_pct} of cited sentences made a claim the page doesn't support, depending on which model did the checking. These test pages don't directly answer the question asked — the situation where misattribution is most likely — so pages that do may fare better.
text.for_you: Check what engines actually say when they cite you, not just whether they do.

findings.title: Tracking tools that query the API may undercount your citations

data.metric: 1 − mean Jaccard similarity of cited-domain sets, API vs logged-out UI

questions.q: Cost to install a home EV charger
Calories in a Chipotle burrito bowl
How long a 5-year ARM stays fixed

body: Most citation-tracking tools query engines through their API. We asked the same {n_questions} everyday questions through OpenAI's API and on chatgpt.com without an account. On {n_web_only} questions the API cited nothing while the website cited real sources. The reverse {reverse_phrase}, and when both cited, they largely pointed to the same sites.
text.note: API: {api_runs_word} runs per question, sources pooled. Website: {ui_runs_word} run. The website may use a different model than the API, so some of the gap could be the model rather than the channel.
text.for_you: If a monitoring tool queries the API, read its citation counts as a floor rather than a measurement of what people see.
prov: Perplexity untestable: its site requires sign-in to search

findings.title: The effect holds on questions we have never released
findings.lever: Replace vague claims with specific figures — on unseen questions

chart.aria: Change in citation rate from adding specific figures, on held-out questions, per engine, with 95% intervals

body: A benchmark that publishes its own corpus is eventually trained on it, and an effect that survives only on questions a model has already seen is not an effect. So a second set of questions was built and deliberately never released — not in this repository, not in any report, not now and not later. Only totals from it are ever published.

Running both sets together, the strongest finding on this page holds on the unreleased half: {pooled_delta_pts} points {pooled_ci_pts}, with an interval clear of zero on every engine. Which half a question came from explains one hundredth of one percent of the variance in whether its page gets cited; the change to the page itself explains a quarter.
text.caption: Change in citation rate from adding specific figures, measured only on questions that have never been published, with 95% intervals. Pooled across {n_models} engines, weighted by market share. {prompts} held-out questions.
after: This is not yet a test for contamination, and the pre-registration says so: at the time of measurement the repository had never been public, so neither set had been exposed and there was no asymmetry to find. What it establishes is the before — a reading that can only be taken once, and that a later re-run is compared against.

One caveat travels with the number. The treatment arm saturates: on most engines every single run cites the page once it carries the figures. So {pooled_delta_pts} is a floor on the effect rather than a measurement of it, and the true size is not identified at this baseline.

The figure above uses a rule corrected after this round was pre-registered. The committed version of the rule dropped any engine that often cited nothing at all, without checking whether that happened only when no page answered the question. One engine was dropped on exactly that basis, and it turned out to show the largest effect here. The pre-registered figure, computed without it, was lower; both numbers and the reason they differ are set out in the report, and the correction now applies to every round.
text.for_you: The advice does not depend on the test set. Adding the specific figure works on questions nobody has optimised against.
prov: held-out half reported as totals only, permanently

story.title: What gets a page cited by AI — OpenGEO
story.description: An open experiment on what makes AI answer engines cite a page: what was tested, what moved citation, how sure we are, and how to run the same test on your own page.
eyebrow: an open experiment on AI answer engines
story.headline: Most advice on getting cited by AI has never been tested. We tested it.
story.standfirst: We put {facts_prompts} everyday questions to {facts_n_models} AI models, {facts_calls} times in all, changing one thing at a time on the pages they could cite. One change stood out: stating the specific answer. Formatting tricks and padding made no difference we could detect. Below is what we found, how sure we are, where the evidence stops, and how to run the same test on your own page.

hero.before: A page that talks around the question
hero.after: The same page, stating the specific answer
hero.note: Averaged over {facts_prompts} questions and {facts_n_models} models. It measures what an engine does once it has the page, not whether it finds it; more on that below.

example.heading: One question, two versions of a page
example.lead: Here are two of the {facts_prompts} questions. Each page came in two versions, and everything else the engine saw was identical: five other pages, in a shuffled order. Each engine answered {runs_per_cell} times per version.

labels.engines: How many of its {runs_per_cell} answers cited the page

example.after: Real answers, quoted as written. In both examples the before answer says the sources don't give the figure, and the after answer quotes the page and cites it. Both questions sit close to the average across all {facts_prompts}; on others the change mattered more, or less.

all.heading: It held on every model we tested
body: Averaged over every question, stating the specific answer raised the share of answers citing the page by {s_facts_pts} points (95% interval {s_facts_ci}). It went up on all {facts_n_models} models we tested, including the five below.

We then repeated it, pre-registered this time, on {heldout_prompts} questions that have never been published anywhere, so no model could have seen them in training: {s_heldout_pts} points ({s_heldout_ci}), up on every engine.
all.caveat: How big it is depends on your competition. In these tests the before page didn't answer the question at all, and the after page was usually the only one that did, so it ended up cited almost every time. Against competitors that already state the answer, expect a smaller gain. The direction is solid; the size is specific to the setup.
all.caption: Share of answers citing the page, per engine, before and after. Engines ordered by share of AI-assistant traffic ({share_source}).

rest.heading: The usual advice barely moved it
body: We tested the other things AI-visibility advice sells, on the same kind of pages and the same scale.

rows.label: State the specific answer
rows.tag: Found twice · held on unpublished questions

rows.label: Answer first, FAQ headings, attribution, citations

rest.caption: Change in the share of answers citing the page, in percentage points, with 95% intervals.
after: Repeating your keyword helped a little: {s_stuffing_pts} points ({s_stuffing_ci}), pre-registered. It's real, but about {stuffing_ratio_vs_compare} times smaller than stating the answer.
Padding a page to twice its length with filler did nothing on average ({s_length_pts} points, {s_length_ci}), and on some engines it cost citations.

Presentation, meaning answer-first order, FAQ-style headings, attributing claims and citing sources, moved citation by {s_presentation_pts} points ({s_presentation_ci}). That comes from an early probe of {presentation_prompts} questions, so read it as nothing found yet, not proof that it never helps.
FAQ schema, the markup, was never tested, and this experiment can't test it: the engines here read a page's visible text, and markup doesn't carry into it.

more.heading: Being cited isn't the whole story

cards.title: Engines sometimes credit you with things you didn't say
cards.text: When an answer cited a page, we checked each cited claim against the page. Between {misattribution_low_pct} and {misattribution_high_pct} of cited sentences said something the page doesn't support, depending on which model did the checking.

cards.title: Tools that check the API may undercount you
cards.text: On {calibration_n_web_only} of {calibration_n_questions} everyday questions, OpenAI's API cited nothing while chatgpt.com cited real sources. Most citation trackers query the API.

cards.title: The engines largely agree
cards.text: Engines agree with each other about which pages deserve a citation about as closely as one engine agrees with itself on a re-run. A page that earns citations from one tends to earn them from the others.

limits.heading: What this can't tell you
steps: The engine searches and picks pages
It reads them and writes an answer
items: Whether an engine finds your page. We hand each engine the pages and measure what it does with them. For many small businesses getting found is the bigger problem, and it's a different experiment.
Local and "near me" searches. The questions were informational (how much, how long, how often), not "best plumber near me".
Exactly what people see in the apps. Each engine is tested through its API, as one model: ChatGPT is OpenAI's {chatgpt_model}, for instance. The apps can behave differently.
Perplexity. It runs its own live search and ignores pages handed to it, so it can't be tested this way.
Real, published pages. The test pages were written for the experiment, so that exactly one thing changes between versions.

test.heading: Run the same test on your own page
body: opengeo test puts your page, as it is and with your change, among your competitors' pages. It asks {engine_names} your question {runs_per_cell} times each, and tells you whether the change moved how often you're cited, per engine, with an interval. It measures what your change did; it never tells you what to change.
It costs {cost_per_question} per question on your own OpenRouter account, and runs every check for free before anything is spent.
test.demo_caption: A real test, on fictional pages for a running-shoe store: the edit swapped one sentence for specific advice on when to replace shoes.
test.command:
python3 opengeo.py test \
    --question "How often should I replace my running shoes?" \
    --page  current.html \
    --edit  edited.html \
    --against comp1.html comp2.html comp3.html comp4.html comp5.html
test.skill: Or ask Claude. The OpenGEO skill gathers your page, your question and your competitors, shows you the cost, runs the test and explains the result: “Test whether adding our prices to our water heater page helps us get cited.”

story.footer: Every figure on this page is read from results/findings.json, which cites the committed report each one comes from; the worked examples are quoted from the raw results and checked against them at every build. Code MIT, data and results CC-BY 4.0.
